subject: Copywriting
title: Writing for Scanners
description: A 60-second lesson on Writing for Scanners.

hook.text: 79% of people scan emails instead of reading them. Scanners look for bolded words, short paragraphs, and bullets.

buildup.text: Nielsen's F-pattern research: eyes scan the first line, then jump down left. Your structure must match this behavior.

discovery.text: One idea per paragraph. Two to three sentences max. White space between blocks. Scanners need visual breathing room.

twist.text: Long emails can work IF formatted for scanners.

climax.text: The best email copywriters write twice: once for readers, then reformat for scanners. Both audiences in one email.

punchline.text: 79% scan, not read. Format for scanning, not perfection.

quiz.question: What reading pattern do email scanners follow?

details.summary: The average reader spends just 11 seconds on a marketing email. Effective email copy is designed for scanners: short paragraphs, bold key phrases, bullet points, and clear visual hierarchy ensure the core message reaches readers who will never read every word.
details.whyItMatters: Writing for scanners is not dumbing down — it is respecting reality. Optimizing for scanning ensures that even the quickest glance communicates the essential message and CTA.
takeaways: Average email reading time is just 11 seconds
Short paragraphs and bold text guide the scanner's eye
Bullet points convey multiple benefits faster than prose paragraphs

faq.question: How do you write emails that work for both scanners and readers?
faq.answer: Use bold text and subheadings that tell the complete story on their own. Scanners get the key points from bold text alone. Readers who want more can dive into the supporting paragraphs. This layered approach serves both audiences simultaneously.

faq.question: What is the ideal paragraph length for marketing emails?
faq.answer: Two to three sentences per paragraph in marketing emails. Single-sentence paragraphs add emphasis and white space. On mobile — where most emails are read — long paragraphs become walls of text that feel overwhelming and trigger scrolling past.
